scope: Authored selected-use comparisons. Group membership does not grant answer credit.

sections.title: To finish
sections.text: Terminar, acabar and concluir overlap for finishing an activity. Acabar de + infinitive also describes something just done; that construction is different.

sections.title: To use
sections.text: Usar, utilizar and emplear all work for using a tool. Emplear also means employ a person; that extra sense is not shared by all three.

sections.title: To happen
sections.text: Ocurrir, suceder and pasar overlap for events happening. Pasar has many other senses, including passing and spending time.

sections.title: Different
sections.text: Diferente and distinto overlap for things that are not the same. Distinto can also emphasize distinctness; neither requires total opposition.

sections.title: To answer
sections.text: Responder and contestar overlap when answering a question. Responder de means answer for or take responsibility for something.

sections.title: To add
sections.text: Agregar and añadir overlap for adding an item. Incluir, incorporar and sumar also fit adding a name to a list. Sumar is not restricted to arithmetic; its broader uses include adding people or things to a whole.
examples: Añade otro nombre a la lista.
Add another name to the list.

sections.title: To understand
sections.text: Comprender and entender overlap for understanding. Comprender can also mean include or comprise; that sense is separate from understanding.

sections.title: To need
sections.text: Necesitar and requerir overlap in the sense of needing. Requerir can also mean formally request or demand; these additional uses are not interchangeable in every sentence.

sections.title: To increase
sections.text: Aumentar and incrementar both describe an increase in an amount. Crecer usually presents the subject itself as growing, rather than directly increasing an object.

sections.title: To reduce
sections.text: Reducir and disminuir overlap when making an amount smaller. Disminuir can also be intransitive: la presión disminuye.

sections.title: To cause
sections.text: Causar, provocar and ocasionar can describe causing a problem. Provocar also means provoke a person; that additional meaning is not automatic for the other verbs.

sections.title: To choose
sections.text: Elegir, escoger and seleccionar overlap for choosing an option. Elegir also describes electing someone to office.

sections.title: To send
sections.text: Enviar and mandar overlap for sending a letter. Mandar also means command; enviar does not carry that sense.

sections.title: To return
sections.text: Regresar, volver and retornar overlap for returning to a place. Volver a + infinitive means do something again; regresar does not substitute for that repeated-action construction.

sections.title: To walk
sections.text: Caminar and andar overlap for walking. Andar also describes how something works or how someone is doing.

sections.title: To find
sections.text: Hallar and encontrar overlap for finding something. Encontrarse also describes meeting someone or being in a state; these uses need their own construction.

sections.title: To hide
sections.text: Esconder and ocultar overlap for hiding something. Ocultar also readily describes concealing information.

sections.title: To cross
sections.text: Cruzar and atravesar overlap for going across a street. Cruzar also describes crossing one's legs; atravesar can describe piercing or going through something.

sections.title: To provide
sections.text: Proporcionar and brindar can mean provide help. Ofrecer can merely offer it, without its being received, so the offer and provision senses need to be kept apart.

sections.title: To continue
sections.text: Continuar and seguir overlap for continuing an activity. Seguir also means follow; that sense is separate.

sections.title: To remain
sections.text: Permanecer means remain. Quedarse commonly expresses staying behind or staying in a place; plain quedar has other uses, such as something remaining available.

sections.title: To obtain
sections.text: Obtener, conseguir and lograr overlap for obtaining a result. Conseguir and lograr commonly take an infinitive directly to mean manage to do something. A useful pattern with obtener is obtener un resultado.

sections.title: To start
sections.text: Iniciar, empezar and comenzar can start an activity expressed as a noun. Empezar and comenzar use a before an infinitive; iniciar does not replace them in that pattern.

sections.title: To place
sections.text: Colocar, poner, situar and ubicar overlap for placing something. Their broader uses differ: poner has many change-of-state constructions, and situar/ubicar emphasize location.
examples: Coloca la mesa junto a la ventana.
Place the table next to the window.

sections.title: To remove
sections.text: Quitar and retirar overlap for removing something. Sacar specifically suggests taking it out of somewhere; not every removal has that direction.
examples: Retira el vaso de la mesa.
Remove the glass from the table.

sections.title: To stop
sections.text: Detener and parar overlap when stopping a vehicle. Detener also means detain someone; detenerse is the usual reflexive form when the subject stops.

sections.title: To throw
sections.text: Echar, lanzar and tirar can describe throwing a ball. Tirar also means throw away, and tirar de means pull on; echar has many fixed expressions.

sections.title: To include
sections.text: Incluir, incorporar, agregar, añadir and sumar all fit adding a name to a list. Integrar emphasizes bringing parts into a whole; integration can involve more than listing something as included.
examples: Incluye su nombre en la lista.
Include his name on the list.

sections.title: To show
sections.text: Mostrar and enseñar overlap when letting someone see something. Enseñar also means teach, which is a different use.

sections.title: To indicate
sections.text: Señalar and indicar can both point out a location. Señalar can involve a gesture or marking; indicar can also give instructions.
examples: Indica el lugar en el mapa.
Indicate the place on the map.

sections.title: To express
sections.text: Expresar and manifestar overlap for expressing an opinion. Manifestar can also make a condition evident; manifestarse can mean demonstrate in public.

sections.title: To guarantee
sections.text: Garantizar and asegurar overlap in giving assurance. Asegurar also means secure physically or insure; those uses require their own context.

sections.title: To state
sections.text: Afirmar emphasizes asserting truth. Declarar can be a statement, especially a formal one; a declaration need not be a claim of certainty.
examples: She states that it is true.

sections.title: To assert
sections.text: Afirmar asserts something as true. Declarar can also state it, often formally; it does not always imply certainty.

sections.title: To declare
sections.text: Declarar can make a statement; afirmar asserts. Declarar also has special uses such as declaring income or declaring love.

sections.title: To suggest
sections.text: Proponer and sugerir overlap for putting forward an idea. Sugerir can also mean imply or evoke something without explicitly proposing it.

sections.title: To keep
sections.text: Conservar and mantener overlap for keeping something in a condition. Guardar emphasizes keeping or storing it; storage does not necessarily mean preservation.
examples: Conserva los documentos en buen estado.
Keep the documents in good condition.

sections.title: To care for
sections.text: Cuidar and atender overlap in looking after someone. Atender can also mean attend to a request; asistir a means attend an event.

sections.title: To attend
sections.text: Asistir a and acudir a overlap for attendance. Atender usually means pay attention to or look after, rather than simply be present at an event.

sections.title: To contribute
sections.text: Aportar commonly takes the contribution as its object. Contribuir commonly uses a for the goal and con for what is contributed; the verbs are not mechanically interchangeable in a fixed sentence.

sections.title: To possess
sections.text: Poseer and tener overlap for possession. Tener is also used for age, sensations and obligations; those constructions do not all transfer to poseer.

sections.title: To love
sections.text: Amar and querer overlap for loving a person. Querer also means want; amar does not replace it in requests or intentions.
examples: She loves her family very much.

sections.title: To want
sections.text: Desear and querer overlap for wishing for something. Querer also expresses affection; that meaning needs a person or other appropriate object.

sections.title: To buy
sections.text: Comprar means buy. Adquirir can mean acquire by purchase but also by other means, so acquire alone does not entail payment.

sections.title: To break
sections.text: Romper and quebrar overlap for breaking a solid object. Quebrar also describes bankruptcy; romper has a wider range of everyday collocations.

sections.title: To transform
sections.text: Transformar expresses a change of form or nature. Cambiar is broader: a change need not amount to a transformation.
examples: Transforma el edificio en un museo.
She transforms the building into a museum.

sections.title: To change
sections.text: Cambiar, alterar and modificar overlap in changing an arrangement. Transformar implies a change in form or nature, which may be more substantial.

sections.title: To constitute
sections.text: Formar, constituir and conformar overlap when parts make up a whole. Conformarse con means settle for; it is a different construction.
examples: Three people make up the team.

sections.title: To clarify
sections.text: Aclarar can clarify an unclear point. Explicar describes explaining it; an explanation can clarify, but the two verbs have other distinct uses.

sections.title: To check
sections.text: Comprobar and verificar overlap in checking correctness. Revisar means examine or review and does not itself promise confirmation.

sections.title: To analyze
sections.text: Analizar emphasizes examining parts or relationships. Examinar and estudiar also fit examining something in detail; examinar can additionally describe a simpler inspection.

sections.title: To investigate
sections.text: Investigar and indagar overlap in investigating a matter. Investigar also covers scientific research.

sections.title: To refuse
sections.text: Rechazar and rehusar overlap for declining an offer. Rechazar also means reject as invalid or repel.

sections.title: To grant
sections.text: Otorgar and conceder overlap for granting permission or an award. These are more specific than simply giving an object.

sections.title: To protect
sections.text: Proteger and defender overlap for protection. Defender emphasizes defending against a threat and also applies to arguing for a position.

sections.title: To help
sections.text: Ayudar and auxiliar overlap in helping someone. Auxiliar often appears in assistance or rescue contexts; ayudar is the general everyday verb.

sections.title: To fight
sections.text: Luchar and combatir overlap for fighting. Luchar commonly takes contra; combatir can take the threat directly as its object.

sections.title: To win
sections.text: Ganar and vencer overlap for being victorious. Ganar also means earn money; vencer can take the defeated opponent directly.

sections.title: To gather
sections.text: Reunir and juntar overlap for bringing things together. Reunirse and juntarse describe people getting together.

sections.title: To separate
sections.text: Separar and apartar overlap for moving things apart. Separar also divides a whole into parts; apartar emphasizes setting something aside.

sections.title: To move
sections.text: Trasladar specifies transfer to another place. Mover also covers motion without a change of location, such as moving an arm.
examples: Trasladan los muebles a otra casa.
They move the furniture to another house.

sections.title: To drive
sections.text: Conducir and manejar overlap for driving a car; manejar is common for this use in much of the Americas. Manejar also means handle or manage.

sections.title: To inform
sections.text: Informar a alguien de algo and comunicar algo a alguien both convey information, with different object patterns. Comunicar also covers communication more broadly.

sections.title: To reveal
sections.text: Revelar means make hidden information known. Descubrir can mean uncover it or discover it for oneself; learning a fact and announcing it are different events.

sections.title: To agree
sections.text: Acordar means agree or decide together. Acordarse de means remember and overlaps with recordar; removing se changes the verb's use.

sections.title: To abandon
sections.text: Abandonar emphasizes leaving behind or giving up. Dejar also means leave, let or lend; those broader uses are not all abandonment.

sections.title: To try
sections.text: Intentar takes an infinitive directly. Tratar de + infinitive also means try to; probar can mean test, taste or try something out.
examples: She tries to open the door.

sections.title: To solve
sections.text: Resolver and solucionar overlap for solving a problem. Resolver can also mean decide or settle a matter.

sections.title: End
sections.text: Fin and final overlap for an ending. Término can also mean end, while conclusión may be a conclusion reached by reasoning; those broader senses need context.
examples: El final de la película es triste.
The end of the film is sad.

sections.title: Beginning
sections.text: Principio, inicio and comienzo overlap for a beginning. Principio also means a principle; that ethical or theoretical sense is separate.
examples: El inicio del curso es mañana.

sections.title: Result
sections.text: Resultado, consecuencia and efecto overlap for outcomes of actions. Resultado also names a score, and efecto has scientific and legal uses that need their own context.
examples: Fue una consecuencia de la decisión.
It was a consequence of the decision.

sections.title: Reason
sections.text: Motivo and razón overlap for a reason to act. Causa names what produces an effect, which need not be someone's conscious motive.
examples: Explica el motivo de su decisión.
She explains the reason for her decision.

sections.title: Goal
sections.text: Objetivo and meta overlap for an aim. Propósito also names an intention; the intended purpose and a measurable target need not be identical.

sections.title: Concept
sections.text: Concepto is a concept or notion. Idea is broader and can be a proposal or thought, so not every idea is a defined concept.

sections.title: Name
sections.text: Nombre and denominación overlap for the name of something. Denominación often concerns a designation or category; nombre is also a person's name.
examples: I do not remember the name.

sections.title: Area
sections.text: Zona, área and región overlap for geographical areas. Región often suggests a larger or recognized territory; área also names a surface measurement.

sections.title: Place
sections.text: Sitio and lugar overlap for a place. Sitio also appears in sitio web, while lugar has expressions such as tener lugar, meaning take place.

sections.title: Route
sections.text: Camino, ruta and vía overlap as ways of reaching a destination. Camino can be a physical path; vía can also be a means or railway track.

sections.title: Way
sections.text: Modo, manera and forma overlap for a way of doing something. Forma also describes shape; modo has grammatical uses.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Método and procedimiento overlap for a way of carrying out a task. Procedimiento often highlights the steps; método can describe the overall approach.

sections.title: Power
sections.text: Poder names power or authority. Fuerza is force or strength; it may contribute to power but is not the same as legal authority.
examples: She has the power to decide.

sections.title: Price
sections.text: Precio is the selling price. Costo/coste is a cost, and valor is value or worth; these amounts can differ.

sections.title: Cost
sections.text: Costo and coste both mean cost, with regional preferences. Gasto is expenditure: money actually spent or an expense.

sections.title: Ability
sections.text: Capacidad and habilidad overlap for ability. Habilidad often emphasizes skill, while capacidad can also be capacity or potential.
examples: She has a skill for drawing.

sections.title: Illness
sections.text: Enfermedad and dolencia overlap for illness. Dolencia can also describe an ailment or complaint without naming a specific disease.

sections.title: School
sections.text: Escuela and colegio overlap for schools, with differences in local education systems. Colegio can also be a professional association; universidad is a different educational level.

sections.title: Teacher
sections.text: Profesor and maestro overlap for a teacher. Maestro also means master or expert, and the preferred term for a schoolteacher varies by place and level.

sections.title: Student
sections.text: Estudiante and alumno overlap for a school student. Alumno emphasizes the relationship to a teacher or institution; estudiante emphasizes studying.

sections.title: Doctor
sections.text: Médico and doctor overlap for a physician. Doctor also refers to a person with a doctorate, who need not be a physician.
examples: La médica trabaja en el hospital.
The doctor works at the hospital.

sections.title: Company
sections.text: Compañía and empresa overlap for a company. Negocio is a business or commercial activity and can also mean a deal; compañía also means companionship.
examples: She works at a small company.

sections.title: Leader
sections.text: Líder and dirigente overlap for a leader. Jefe emphasizes being in charge or holding authority; a leader need not be someone's boss.
examples: He is the leader of the group.

sections.title: Job
sections.text: Trabajo, empleo and puesto overlap for a job. Trabajo also means work generally, while puesto emphasizes a particular position.
examples: She is looking for a job.

sections.title: Task
sections.text: Tarea names a task; labor and trabajo can describe the work involved. Trabajo also names employment, while una tarea can be unpaid or schoolwork.

sections.title: Act
sections.text: Acto and acción overlap for an act. Hecho can name a deed but also a fact or event, whether or not someone deliberately did it.
examples: It was an act of generosity.

sections.title: Piece of information
sections.text: Dato is an individual item of information. Información is usually the information as a whole; datos is the plural corresponding to data.
examples: One piece of information is missing.

sections.title: Answer
sections.text: Respuesta and contestación overlap for a reply. Respuesta can also describe a reaction to an event rather than a verbal answer.
examples: I am waiting for your answer.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: Pregunta directly names a question asked. Cuestión may be a question under discussion, and asunto/tema mean a matter or topic rather than necessarily a question sentence.

sections.title: Matter
sections.text: Asunto, cuestión and tema overlap for a matter under discussion. Tema also means a theme or topic, and cuestión can be a question or problem.

sections.title: Film
sections.text: Película and filme overlap for a film. Película also means a thin layer, so that physical meaning needs separate treatment.

sections.title: Photograph
sections.text: Foto is a shortened form of fotografía and remains feminine: una foto. Fotografía also names photography as an activity or art.

sections.title: Face
sections.text: Cara and rostro overlap for a face. Rostro can sound more formal or literary; cara also means a side or surface.

sections.title: Ground
sections.text: Suelo, tierra and terreno overlap in ground-related senses. Tierra can mean soil or land; terreno emphasizes a tract or type of land, and suelo also means a floor. Both tierra and suelo fit the selected soil cue: earth that supports plant growth.

sections.title: Floor
sections.text: Piso and suelo overlap for a floor surface. Piso also names a storey or an apartment in some regions; those meanings are separate.
examples: El suelo de la cocina está limpio.

sections.title: Room
sections.text: Habitación and cuarto overlap for a room. Sala commonly names a larger or public room or a living room; not every room is a sala.

sections.title: Home
sections.text: Casa and hogar overlap for home. Vivienda emphasizes a dwelling or housing; hogar also evokes home life and can mean hearth.

sections.title: Car
sections.text: Coche, automóvil and carro can name a car, with regional preferences. Carro can also be a cart, so its meaning depends on place and context.

sections.title: Husband
sections.text: Marido and esposo both mean husband. Novio means boyfriend or groom and does not by itself mean husband.

sections.title: Mom
sections.text: Mamá is a familiar form of madre. Madre is the neutral relationship term; mamá has final stress and an accent.

sections.title: Dad
sections.text: Papá is a familiar form of padre. Papá has final stress; papa without the accent can mean potato or pope.

sections.title: Boy
sections.text: Chico and muchacho overlap for a boy or young person. Niño specifically suggests a child; the applicable age range depends on context. Niño also fits boy when the person is a child; chico and muchacho can extend to adolescents and young men.

sections.title: Food
sections.text: Comida and alimento overlap for food. Comida also means a meal, whereas alimento can be one foodstuff or nourishment.

sections.title: Meeting
sections.text: Reunión and encuentro can name a meeting. Sesión is a scheduled period of activity and need not be a meeting; encuentro can also be an accidental encounter.
examples: La reunión empieza a las diez.

sections.title: Event
sections.text: Evento, suceso and acontecimiento overlap for an event. Evento often names an organized occasion; suceso can refer to an incident.

sections.title: Opportunity
sections.text: Ocasión and oportunidad overlap for a chance. Ocasión can also mean an occasion or time when something happens, without implying a favorable opportunity.

sections.title: Danger
sections.text: Peligro emphasizes danger; riesgo often emphasizes the possibility or exposure to harm. They overlap in ordinary speech but are distinguished in technical contexts. Both are accepted for these ordinary-language cues; no technical distinction is specified.
examples: There is a danger of fire.

sections.title: Memory
sections.text: Recuerdo is a specific memory. Memoria also names the faculty of remembering or stored information; those broader meanings do not all take recuerdo.
examples: Es un recuerdo de mi infancia.
It is a memory from my childhood.

sections.title: Freedom
sections.text: Libertad is freedom. Independencia means independence from control or dependence; a particular freedom is not necessarily complete independence.

sections.title: Increase
sections.text: Aumento and incremento overlap for an increase. Crecimiento is growth, which may be physical, numerical or developmental.
examples: There was an increase in prices.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: Conclusión can be a reasoned conclusion or an ending. Fin names an end or purpose, not a reasoned judgment.

sections.title: Victory
sections.text: Victoria and triunfo overlap for victory. Triunfo can also describe success more generally, without a specific opponent.

sections.title: Mistake
sections.text: Error and equivocación overlap for a mistake. Error also has technical meanings in measurement or computation.

sections.title: Stage
sections.text: Etapa and fase overlap for stages of a process. Etapa also names a leg of a journey or race.

sections.title: Moment
sections.text: Instante and momento overlap for a short moment. Momento also means a particular time or occasion and need not imply an instant.

sections.title: Newspaper
sections.text: Periódico and diario overlap for a newspaper. Diario can also mean diary, and as an adjective means daily.

sections.title: Daily
sections.text: Diario and cotidiano overlap for daily. Periódico means recurring at intervals, not necessarily every day.

sections.title: Story
sections.text: Relato, cuento and historia overlap for a story. Cuento commonly names a short fictional tale; historia also means history, and relato need not be fictional.

sections.title: Sound
sections.text: Sonido is sound in general. Ruido often means noise, especially unwanted or irregular sound; not every sound is ruido.
examples: Oigo un ruido en la calle.
I hear a noise in the street.

sections.title: Feeling
sections.text: Sentimiento and emoción overlap for emotional experience. Sensación often describes a bodily sensation or impression; those are not automatically emotions.

sections.title: Soul
sections.text: Alma and espíritu overlap in spiritual senses. Espíritu also names attitude or disposition; alma takes el when the article directly precedes its stressed initial a in the singular but is feminine.
examples: She talks about the human soul.

sections.title: Spirit; soul
sections.text: Espíritu and alma overlap for soul or spirit. Espíritu also refers to attitude, disposition or a ghost; those senses need separate context.

sections.title: Soul
sections.text: Alma is feminine despite el alma in the singular. Espíritu overlaps in the spiritual-being sense but has other meanings.

sections.title: Rule
sections.text: Regla and norma overlap for a rule governing behavior. Regla also means ruler, and norma can be a customary norm rather than an explicit instruction.

sections.title: Medicine
sections.text: Medicina and medicamento overlap for a medicinal substance. Medicina also names the field of medicine; medicamento does not.

sections.title: Language
sections.text: Lengua and idioma overlap for a named language. Lenguaje can describe the human faculty, a system of expression or a style of language; it need not identify a national language.

sections.title: Exhibition
sections.text: Exposición and muestra overlap for an exhibition. Muestra also means a sample, while exposición has senses of explanation and exposure.

sections.title: Environment
sections.text: Ambiente and entorno overlap for surroundings. Ambiente also names an atmosphere or mood; entorno emphasizes what surrounds a person or thing.

sections.title: Feature
sections.text: Característica and rasgo overlap for a distinguishing trait. Rasgo also describes a stroke or facial feature.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.text: Prueba can be evidence, proof or a test. Evidencia can name evidence or obviousness; taking a test is not expressed by substituting evidencia for prueba.

sections.title: Advice
sections.text: Consejo and recomendación overlap for advice. Recomendación can also be an endorsement; consejo is countable in Spanish: un consejo.
examples: I will give you a piece of advice.

sections.title: Desire
sections.text: Deseo names a desire. Ganas is common in tener ganas de, meaning feel like doing something; voluntad also means will or willingness.

sections.title: Near
sections.text: Próximo and cercano overlap for spatial nearness. Próximo also means next; cercano does not replace it in every future-time expression.

sections.title: Next
sections.text: Siguiente and próximo overlap for what comes next. Próximo also means near; siguiente always involves a sequence.
examples: La próxima reunión es el lunes.
The next meeting is on Monday.

sections.title: Previous
sections.text: Anterior and previo overlap for something earlier. Anterior also describes a position at the front in anatomical or spatial uses.

sections.title: Current
sections.text: Actual and presente overlap for current. Actual does not normally mean actual in the English sense of real; presente also means present rather than absent.

sections.title: Real
sections.text: Real and verdadero overlap for genuine or real. Verdadero also means true rather than false; real can also mean royal.

sections.title: True
sections.text: Cierto and verdadero overlap for true. Before a noun, cierto can mean a certain or some, which does not assert truth.

sections.title: Obvious
sections.text: Claro, evidente and obvio overlap for something obvious. Claro also means clear, pale or light; those senses are distinct.

sections.title: Simple
sections.text: Simple and sencillo overlap for uncomplicated. Sencillo also suggests plain or unpretentious; simple has other senses, including mere.

sections.title: Difficult
sections.text: Difícil and complicado overlap for something hard to do. Complicado can specifically mean complex, so not every difficult task is complicated.

sections.title: Easy
sections.text: Fácil means easy. Sencillo can be easy or uncomplicated, but a simple task can still require great effort.

sections.title: Strange
sections.text: Extraño and raro overlap for strange. Raro also means rare; extraño can mean foreign or unfamiliar.

sections.title: Famous
sections.text: Famoso means famous. Conocido means known and can refer to a familiar person or fact without widespread fame.

sections.title: Fundamental
sections.text: Básico and fundamental overlap for foundational importance. Básico can also mean elementary rather than advanced.

sections.title: Specific
sections.text: Específico, concreto, particular and determinado overlap in identifying something specific. Particular and determinado also have other meanings; concreto can mean concrete rather than abstract.

sections.title: Main
sections.text: Principal and primordial overlap for primary importance. Principal can also name the main item in an arrangement, not necessarily something fundamental in origin.

sections.title: Usual
sections.text: Habitual, normal and común overlap for what is usual. Normal can refer to a standard, and común can mean shared; neither always means frequent.

sections.title: Frequent
sections.text: Frecuente means frequent. Habitual can mean customary even when something happens only occasionally on a regular schedule.

sections.title: Global
sections.text: Mundial and global overlap for worldwide scope. Global can also mean overall, considering something as a whole rather than worldwide.

sections.title: Safe
sections.text: Seguro can mean safe or secure. Protegido means protected; protection is a means of safety, not a guarantee of it. Seguro also means certain.

sections.title: Fast
sections.text: Rápido and veloz overlap for fast movement. Rápido also describes something taking little time.

sections.title: Large
sections.text: Grande is general size. Enorme emphasizes very large, while amplio emphasizes breadth or spaciousness; they are not always equivalent degrees or dimensions.

sections.title: Strong
sections.text: Fuerte and intenso overlap for intensity, such as pain or heat. Fuerte also means physically strong; intenso does not usually describe muscular strength.

sections.title: Serious
sections.text: Grave and serio overlap for a serious problem. Serio can also describe a person's sober manner, while grave can describe a low-pitched sound.

sections.title: Full
sections.text: Lleno describes something filled. Completo means complete, with nothing missing; pleno can mean full or complete in particular combinations, but does not replace lleno for every container.

sections.title: Old
sections.text: Viejo and antiguo overlap for old objects. Antiguo can mean ancient or former; viejo also refers to old age and can sound blunt when applied to a person.

sections.title: Young
sections.text: Joven is young, or a young person as a noun. Adolescente identifies adolescence specifically; not every young person is an adolescent.

sections.title: Happy
sections.text: Feliz and contento overlap for feeling happy or pleased. Feliz also describes a happy life or fortunate event, beyond a momentary feeling.

sections.title: Calm
sections.text: Tranquilo and calmado overlap for calm. Tranquilo also describes a quiet place, while calmado often suggests composure or agitation having subsided.

sections.title: Free
sections.text: Libre concerns freedom or availability. Gratis means without charge; something can be libre without being gratis, or gratis without being unrestricted.

sections.title: Short
sections.text: Bajo describes low height, including a short person. Corto describes short length or duration; pequeño describes small size more generally.

sections.title: Legal
sections.text: Jurídico concerns law. Legal can mean relating to law or permitted by law; judicial specifically concerns judges and courts.

sections.title: Public
sections.text: Público can mean public or state-run. Estatal specifically relates to the state, and político to politics; these are related concepts, not interchangeable adjectives.

sections.title: Expert
sections.text: Experto is an expert. Especialista specializes in a field, and profesional practices an occupation; the labels overlap but do not guarantee the same expertise.

sections.title: Only
sections.text: Solamente, únicamente and adverbial solo overlap for only. Adjectival solo means alone or sole and agrees with the noun.

sections.title: Still
sections.text: Todavía and aún overlap for still or yet. Aun without the accent can mean even, including; it is a different use.

sections.title: Never
sections.text: Jamás and nunca overlap for never. Negative words following a verb usually combine with no: no viene nunca.

sections.title: Perhaps
sections.text: Quizá and quizás are spelling variants with the same meaning. Acaso can also mean perhaps but has distinct uses in questions and por si acaso.

sections.title: Currently
sections.text: Actualmente and ahora overlap for present time. Ahora can mean right now, while actualmente often covers the current period; actualmente does not mean actually.

sections.title: Really
sections.text: Realmente and verdaderamente overlap for really or genuinely. Actualmente means currently, so it does not substitute for actually in this sense.

sections.title: Also
sections.text: Asimismo and también overlap for also. Asimismo often links statements in formal writing; así mismo can mean in that same way, and a sí mismo means to oneself.

sections.title: Especially
sections.text: Especialmente and particularmente overlap for especially or particularly. The emphasis depends on the sentence, not a strict division between the two.

sections.title: Mainly
sections.text: Principalmente and fundamentalmente overlap for mainly. Fundamentalmente can also mean fundamentally, concerning the basis of something.

sections.title: Finally
sections.text: Finalmente can mean finally or lastly. Por fin emphasizes an awaited outcome and is two words; not every final item carries that sense of relief.

sections.title: Soon
sections.text: Pronto means soon. Temprano means early relative to a schedule or usual time; an early event need not be soon.

sections.title: There
sections.text: Ahí, allí and allá overlap in English as there. Ahí often points to a more immediate or listener-associated place, allí to a more distant specific place, and allá to a less bounded region or direction; usage varies.

sections.title: Above
sections.text: Arriba describes an upper place or direction. Encima commonly uses de for above or on top of a named thing; sobre takes its complement directly.
examples: El libro está encima de la mesa.
The book is on top of the table.

sections.title: Below
sections.text: Abajo describes a lower place or downward direction. Debajo commonly uses de before its complement; bajo takes the complement directly.
examples: El gato está debajo de la mesa.
The cat is under the table.

sections.title: Behind
sections.text: Detrás de explicitly relates a position to something else. Atrás often means backward or at the back and can also describe past time; usage with complements varies regionally.

sections.title: In front
sections.text: Delante de gives a position in front of something. Adelante commonly gives a forward direction or encouragement to proceed.
examples: It is in front of the house.

sections.title: Approximately
sections.text: Cerca de and alrededor de can express approximation. Without that numerical construction, cerca means nearby and alrededor means around.
examples: There are about a hundred people.

sections.title: Even
sections.text: Incluso, adverbial hasta and aun can mean even. Hasta also means until or as far as; aún with an accent means still or yet.

sections.title: To listen to
sections.text: Escuchar emphasizes listening with attention. Oír also has a listen-to use, so both fit this cue; hearing a sound does not necessarily imply paying attention.

sections.title: To hear
sections.text: Oír is the general verb for hearing. Escuchar is also used for perceiving a sound, especially in American usage; attention is a useful tendency, not an absolute acceptance boundary.

sections.title: To play
sections.text: Jugar is used for games and sports. Playing a musical instrument normally uses tocar; the English verb play covers both.

sections.title: To touch
sections.text: Tocar means touch and also play an instrument. Jugar means play a game or sport; it does not replace tocar for physical touch.

sections.title: To learn
sections.text: Aprender is learning or acquiring a skill. Estudiar is studying, which may lead to learning; enseñar is teaching someone else.

sections.title: To study
sections.text: Estudiar describes study; aprender describes learning or acquiring knowledge. The activity and its result are distinct.

sections.title: To take on
sections.text: Here asumir means taking on a duty or responsibility. It can also mean taking something as true, overlapping with suponer; that is a separate sense, not an incorrect use.

sections.title: To suppose
sections.text: Suponer, imaginar and asumir can mean taking something as true. RAE recognizes this use of asumir; its separate take-on-responsibility sense does not exclude the assumption sense.

sections.title: To request
sections.text: Solicitar and pedir request something. Preguntar asks a question; preguntar información does not substitute for pedir información.

sections.title: To drink
sections.text: Beber and tomar both work for drinking a beverage. Tomar has many broader senses, including take; those do not all involve drinking.

sections.title: To save
sections.text: Salvar is saving or rescuing from danger. Guardar is keeping or storing something, such as saving a file.

sections.title: To save
sections.text: Guardar is the usual verb for saving a file. Salvar commonly means rescue; file-saving terminology can vary by software and region.

sections.title: To lend
sections.text: Prestar means lend. Pedir prestado means borrow; lending and borrowing describe opposite sides of the transaction.

sections.title: To hand over
sections.text: Entregar emphasizes delivery or handing over. Dar is broader but also fits giving an object to someone.

sections.title: To bring
sections.text: Traer brings toward a reference point, often the speaker; llevar takes something toward another destination. The viewpoint matters.

sections.title: To bring closer
sections.text: Acercar brings something closer; alejar moves it farther away. Acercarse and alejarse describe the subject approaching or moving away.

sections.title: To move away
sections.text: Alejar increases distance, while acercar reduces it. The reflexive forms describe the subject's own movement.

sections.title: To lift
sections.text: Levantar and alzar lift an object. Subir can also raise or move something upward; its construction depends on the object and destination.

sections.title: To generate
sections.text: Generar and producir overlap for producing energy. Crear is broader creation and is not a substitute in every technical energy context.

sections.title: To build
sections.text: Construir and edificar overlap for buildings. Construir also applies to arguments, machines and other things that are not buildings.

sections.title: To observe
sections.text: Observar emphasizes careful observation. Mirar can also describe watching attentively; ver can simply be visual perception.

sections.title: To appear
sections.text: Aparecer and surgir overlap when something comes into view or emerges. Aparecer also means turn up, including after being missing.

sections.title: To arise
sections.text: Surgir emphasizes emergence or arising. Aparecer can also describe something appearing, without specifying how it developed.

sections.title: To grow
sections.text: Crecer describes a child growing. Aumentar generally concerns an amount or magnitude; a child is not normally the subject of aumentar in this sense.

sections.title: To die
sections.text: Morir is die; matar is kill. Fallecer is a formal alternative for a person's death, and morirse is a common pronominal form.

sections.title: To kill
sections.text: Matar takes the being killed as its object. Morir describes dying, not causing another's death.

sections.title: To laugh
sections.text: Reír means laugh; sonreír means smile. A smile does not necessarily involve laughter.

sections.title: To smile
sections.text: Sonreír means smile, while reír means laugh. They describe related but distinct actions.

sections.title: To notice
sections.text: Notar, advertir and percibir overlap for noticing a change. Advertir also means warn; perceiving something is not necessarily warning someone.

sections.title: To warn
sections.text: Advertir and avisar can warn of danger. Advertir also means notice, but notar does not replace it for warning someone.

sections.title: To perceive
sections.text: Percibir and notar overlap for perceiving a change. Percibir can also mean receive income; that additional sense does not transfer to notar.

sections.title: To prevent
sections.text: Impedir and evitar overlap for preventing an event. Evitar also means avoid something without preventing it from existing.

sections.title: To avoid
sections.text: Evitar and esquivar overlap in avoiding an obstacle. Impedir means prevent or obstruct; it does not mean going around an obstacle oneself.

sections.title: To exhibit
sections.text: Exponer and mostrar overlap for displaying works. Exponer also means explain or expose to a risk; those uses require context.

sections.title: To mention
sections.text: Mencionar and citar overlap when referring to someone or something. Citar can also quote a source or summon a person.

sections.title: To cite
sections.text: Citar can mention a source or quote it. Mencionar means mention; it does not by itself promise exact quotation.

sections.title: To recommend
sections.text: Recomendar and aconsejar overlap for recommending something. Aconsejar also concerns advice about actions.

sections.title: To support
sections.text: Apoyar and respaldar overlap for giving support. Sostener can support physically or maintain an argument; context determines the overlap.

sections.title: To hold up
sections.text: Sostener and sujetar can hold an object in place. Mantener is broader keeping in a state; it does not always describe physical support.

sections.title: To apply
sections.text: Aplicar puts a rule or method into practice. Usar is broader use; the words overlap in some contexts but have different constructions.

sections.title: To work
sections.text: Funcionar describes a machine or system working. Trabajar commonly describes work or labor; it is not a general replacement for funcionar.

sections.title: Worker
sections.text: Trabajador is anyone who works. Empleado is an employee; a self-employed worker need not be an empleado.

sections.title: Employee
sections.text: Empleado specifies an employment relationship. Trabajador is broader and also includes people working independently.

sections.title: Use
sections.text: Uso, utilización and empleo overlap for use. Empleo also means employment or a job; those senses are distinct.

sections.title: Century
sections.text: Siglo and centuria mean century. Década is a decade, ten years.

sections.title: Measurement
sections.text: Medida can be a measurement or a measure taken in response to a problem. Medición concerns measuring; it does not replace medida for a policy measure.

sections.title: Spanish
sections.text: Español and castellano both name the Spanish language. Castellano can also refer specifically to Castile in other uses.

sections.title: Writer
sections.text: Escritor and autor overlap for a writer of literary works. Autor also names the creator of a nonwritten work or the perpetrator of an act.

sections.title: Author
sections.text: Autor and escritor overlap for a book's writer. Autor also applies to other creators; escritor specifically concerns writing.

sections.title: Congress
sections.text: Congreso can be a conference or a legislative body. Conferencia can also be a lecture or conference; the legislative meaning is separate.

sections.title: Conference
sections.text: Conferencia and congreso overlap for conferences. Conferencia also means lecture, while congreso may name a legislature.

sections.title: Purchase
sections.text: Compra is a purchase. Adquisición is broader acquisition, which can occur by purchase or by another means.

sections.title: Advantage
sections.text: Ventaja is an advantage; beneficio can be a benefit. Beneficio also means profit, which is not always a comparative advantage.

sections.title: Benefit
sections.text: Beneficio and ventaja overlap for a benefit or advantage. Financial profit is another sense of beneficio.

sections.title: Chest
sections.text: Pecho and tórax overlap for the chest. Pecho can also mean a breast; tórax names the thorax more broadly.

sections.title: Owner
sections.text: Dueño and propietario overlap for an owner. Propietario is also used as an adjective meaning proprietary or owning.

sections.title: Dead person
sections.text: Muerto, difunto and fallecido can name a deceased person. Muerto also functions as an adjective, distinct from this noun card.

sections.title: Old person
sections.text: Viejo can refer to an old person and may sound blunt. Anciano or una persona mayor can be more neutral or respectful depending on context.

sections.title: Independent
sections.text: Independiente and autónomo overlap for independence. Autónomo also describes self-employment or an autonomous region.

sections.title: Effective
sections.text: Efectivo and eficaz overlap for effective. Efectivo also means real and, as a noun, cash; those are separate uses.

sections.title: Fact
sections.text: Hecho can be a fact, event or deed. Acto is an act; it does not replace hecho in the selected fact sense.

sections.title: Space
sections.text: Espacio can refer to physical space or a span of time. Período names a time interval, not physical distance between objects.

sections.title: To like
sections.text: Gustar uses the liked thing as its subject and the person as an indirect object. Querer means want or love and uses a different construction.

sections.title: Society
sections.text: Sociedad can name society broadly or an association/company. Comunidad is a community; these related concepts are not identical in every context.

sections.title: Sense
sections.text: Sentido can mean a faculty of perception or a direction. Sensación is a sensation, not the faculty itself.

sections.title: Village; town
sections.text: Pueblo and población can name a settlement. Población also means population; nación is a nation rather than necessarily one settlement.

sections.title: Population
sections.text: Población names the population or a settlement. Pueblo can name a settlement or a people; population size is expressed with población.

sections.title: Voice
sections.text: Voz can be a voice or a lexical item. Término can mean a word or term, but not the sound of a speaking voice.

sections.title: Truth
sections.text: Verdad is truth. Hecho can be an individual fact; the concepts overlap but are not interchangeable in every expression.

sections.title: To seat
sections.text: Sentar seats someone; sentarse means sit down. Sentar bases can mean establish foundations, but establecer does not mean seat a person.

sections.title: Resource
sections.text: Recurso and medio overlap for a means. Recurso also means a legal appeal, a separate sense.

sections.title: Experience
sections.text: Experiencia and práctica overlap for experience gained through doing. Una experiencia can also be an individual event someone lived through.

sections.title: Young person
sections.text: Joven can be a young person of any gender. Muchacho generally means a boy or young man; it is not an exact match for an unrestricted person prompt.

sections.title: Production
sections.text: Producción is production, the process or output. Producto is an individual product; process and item should not be confused.

sections.title: Product
sections.text: Producto names a product. Producción describes producing or its output as a whole.

sections.title: Police officer
sections.text: Policía names the police or an officer. Agente can also mean an officer when the context is police, but has broader meanings.

sections.title: Agent
sections.text: Agente can be a representative or a police officer. Policía fits the officer sense, not every kind of agent.

sections.title: War
sections.text: Guerra is war. Conflicto and lucha are broader and can be nonmilitary; related words need not express the same scale or kind of confrontation.

sections.title: Lesson; class
sections.text: Clase can be a lesson, class or kind. Género and tipo overlap only with its kind/category sense.

sections.title: Genre
sections.text: Género names a genre or a kind and also gender. Sexo concerns sex; the terms are not interchangeable across all uses.

sections.title: Eyesight
sections.text: Vista and visión overlap for eyesight. Vista also names a view; visión can name a vision or perspective.

sections.title: Vision
sections.text: Visión and vista overlap for visual ability. A vision of the future is another use of visión.

sections.title: Period
sections.text: Período and época overlap for time periods. Época often evokes an era characterized by events or conditions; duration is determined by context.

sections.title: Era; period
sections.text: Época and período overlap for a time period. Época often evokes a historically or personally characterized era.

sections.title: Source
sections.text: Fuente can be an information source, fountain or spring. Origen overlaps with source as origin, not a physical fountain.

sections.title: Post; position
sections.text: Cargo, puesto and posición overlap for an organizational role. Cargo also means a charge or responsibility; those uses need context.

sections.title: Term
sections.text: Término can be a word or an ending. Fin overlaps with the ending sense, not the lexical-item sense selected here.

sections.title: Object
sections.text: Objeto can be a thing or a purpose. Objetivo is an aim; it does not name every physical object.

sections.title: Being
sections.text: Ser and organismo overlap for a living entity. The noun ser is distinct from the infinitive ser, to be.

sections.title: Plant
sections.text: Planta can be a plant, a factory or a storey. Piso overlaps with storey, not the living-plant sense.

sections.title: Entrance
sections.text: Entrada and acceso overlap for an entrance. Entrada also means admission or a ticket in some contexts.

sections.title: Access
sections.text: Acceso concerns access or a way in. Entrada may name a physical entrance; access can be permission rather than a doorway.

sections.title: Club
sections.text: Club is a kind of association organized around an interest. Asociación is broader and can name other organizations.

sections.title: News item
sections.text: Noticia is news or a news item. Mensaje is a message, which need not report news.

sections.title: To aim
sections.text: Apuntar can mean aim or note down. Indicar and señalar can point something out, but do not substitute in every weapon-aiming construction.

sections.title: Scene
sections.text: Escena is a scene; escenario can be a stage or setting. A performance's scene and its physical stage are distinct.

sections.title: Stage
sections.text: Escenario is a stage or setting. Escena can name a dramatic scene rather than the physical platform.

sections.title: Painting
sections.text: Cuadro can mean painting, chart or a group. Tabla overlaps with a chart, not a painted picture.

sections.title: Painting
sections.text: Pintura can name a painting, painting as an activity or paint. Cuadro fits the individual-artwork sense.

sections.title: Piece
sections.text: Pieza can be a piece or, regionally, a room. Cuarto matches the room sense, not every component.

sections.title: Destination
sections.text: Destino can mean destination or fate. Sino overlaps with fate, not a travel destination.

sections.title: Alive
sections.text: Vivo can mean alive, vivid or lively. Intenso overlaps with vivid intensity, not being biologically alive.

sections.title: Equal
sections.text: Igual expresses equality. Mismo can express identity; equal quantities need not be the very same object.

sections.title: Equally
sections.text: Adverbial igual can mean equally, or perhaps in informal speech. Quizá overlaps only with the possibility sense.

sections.title: Morning
sections.text: As a noun, mañana is morning. As an adverb, mañana means tomorrow; the separate cards retain their parts of speech.

sections.title: Tomorrow
sections.text: Adverbial mañana means tomorrow, while ayer means yesterday. The noun mañana means morning.

sections.title: Afternoon
sections.text: Tarde names the afternoon or early evening, with boundaries varying by place and season. Noche is night; adverbial tarde means late.

sections.title: Late
sections.text: Adverbial tarde means late and contrasts with temprano, early. The noun tarde means afternoon.

sections.title: Working day
sections.text: Jornada commonly names a working day or day's activity. Día is the general word for day and also fits this selected use.

sections.title: Instrument; tool
sections.text: Instrumento and herramienta overlap for a tool or implement. Instrumento also names a musical instrument or a formal document.

sections.title: Tool
sections.text: Herramienta and instrumento overlap for tools. Not every musical instrumento is called a herramienta in ordinary usage.

sections.title: To split
sections.text: Partir can mean split or depart. Salir overlaps with departure, not dividing an object.

sections.title: To take
sections.text: Coger commonly means take in Spain but has a vulgar sexual meaning in many American regions. Tomar is a widely usable alternative for taking.

sections.title: To arrange
sections.text: Ordenar can arrange things or give an order. Mandar overlaps with commanding, not simply arranging objects.

sections.title: Awareness
sections.text: Conciencia can be awareness or conscience. Conocimiento overlaps with knowing or awareness, not moral conscience.

sections.title: Knowledge
sections.text: Conocimiento is knowledge. Conciencia can express awareness or conscience, not all accumulated knowledge.

sections.title: Will
sections.text: Voluntad can mean will, willingness or desire. Deseo names a wish; it need not imply the will to carry it out.

sections.title: To prepare
sections.text: Elaborar and preparar overlap for preparing a report. Elaborar emphasizes working it out or developing it.

sections.title: Tax
sections.text: Impuesto is a tax. Tasa can be a rate or a particular fee; the legal categories vary and are not automatically interchangeable.

sections.title: Rate
sections.text: Tasa can mean a rate or fee. Impuesto is a tax, not a numerical rate itself.

sections.title: Signature
sections.text: Firma can mean a signature or a firm. Empresa overlaps only with the business sense.

sections.title: The present
sections.text: Actualidad is the present or current affairs. Noticia is a news item, not the current time itself.

sections.title: How
sections.text: Qué can intensify an exclamation before an adjective or adverb: qué bien. Cómo has different exclamatory constructions and is not a mechanical replacement.

sections.title: Which one
sections.text: Cuál commonly asks for selection or identification. Qué can ask for a definition or appear before a noun; regional usage and construction affect overlap.

sections.title: To provide
sections.text: Facilitar can mean provide something, such as help or information. It also means make easier; that broader use is distinct.

sections.title: To add
sections.text: Sumar names arithmetic addition and also adding to an amount. Añadir is broader adding; this cue selects arithmetic.

sections.title: Final
sections.text: Final and último overlap for the last item in a sequence. Final also means conclusive; último is also used for latest.

sections.title: Alone
sections.text: Adjectival solo means alone or sole and agrees with its noun. Solamente and adverbial solo mean only; they do not express being without company.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Desenlace fits the ending or resolution of a film; fin and final are broader ending words.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Desenlace fits a film’s ending or resolution. El final means the end; la final means a decisive competition.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Indagación and pesquisa also name an investigation; pesquisa is less usual in everyday conversation.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Fortaleza can describe physical strength as well as inner strength; the physical sense fits here.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Autoridad fits the power or authority to act. Poder also has other senses, such as capability.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Caer and caerse both describe falling; the pronominal form often presents the fall as an event affecting the subject.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Vos is a valid informal singular subject pronoun in voseo varieties; tú is used in tuteo.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Procurar and intentar can both take an infinitive for trying to do something.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Determinación can name a decision, especially in tomar una determinación; it also means resolve.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Centenar and centena name a group of one hundred, like the noun ciento. Cien is the numeral form, not this collective-noun target.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Falta, carencia and escasez overlap for a lack or shortage; escasez emphasizes scarcity.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Resaltar can mean highlight or stand out; sobresalir fits the stand-out sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Plata means money in many American varieties; it also means silver.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Convenio and pacto name agreements, often more specific or formal than acuerdo.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Petiso and chaparro can describe a short person; their frequency and connotations vary by region, and chaparro can suggest a stocky build.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Influir fits the influence sense. Afectar is transitive; influir commonly uses en or sobre before what is influenced.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Niño fits boy when the young person is a child. Chico and muchacho can also refer to older boys or young men.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Padecer and sufrir overlap for suffering an illness or another unwanted experience.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Descender fits going or coming down; bajar has additional transitive uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Both verbs can convey giving someone information: informar a alguien de algo, comunicar algo a alguien. Their complements differ.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Ascender fits going or coming up; subir has additional transitive uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Referir can mean report or recount an event. Informar, reportar, contar and relatar fit the broad report cue; referirse a is a separate construction meaning refer to.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Meter, introducir and insertar fit putting something inside something else; insertar often suggests fitting it into a particular place.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Fuera and afuera overlap for outside; their use with an explicit de complement varies by region.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Usual, común, normal and habitual overlap for customary rather than exceptional.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Período and periodo are both correct for a period of time; the spelling reflects the chosen stress.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Mostrar fits show or demonstrate; probar fits demonstrate in the sense of proving. Their constructions depend on the intended sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Integrante means a member of a group. Miembro also names a body part.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Era fits a period characterized by an event or historical conditions. Período and periodo are both correct for a period of time.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Porvenir names the time ahead, like the noun futuro; it is not the adjective future.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Respaldo fits support or backing. Apoyo also has physical-support uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Vistazo fits a glance, especially echar un vistazo; mirada is broader and can be sustained.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Proposición can mean a proposal; propuesta is often more usual in everyday contexts.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Década and decenio both cover ten years. Década often labels a named decade.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Temor and miedo both express fear; temor can sound more formal.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Cosa fits a physical thing; objeto is more specific when naming a discrete object.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Triunfo can express success as well as victory in a contest.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Grupo fits a group or an ensemble; conjunto also has the mathematical set sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Exceder and sobrepasar fit surpassing or exceeding a limit.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Presentar fits presenting a problem; plantear also means raising or posing it.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Opuesto fits opposite; contrario also has opposing or adverse uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Reporte is also used for a report, especially in American Spanish.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Extremo fits the furthest or terminal end; cabo has additional nautical and geographic senses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Tapar fits covering something; cubrir also has broader figurative uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Vos is used after prepositions in voseo varieties: para vos. Ti belongs to tuteo: para ti.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Lecho is a literary word for bed; cama is the ordinary everyday word.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Comportarse fits behaving; obrar can mean acting or behaving. Actuar also means performing on stage.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Esencial and fundamental can both describe something basic or indispensable.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Fútbol and futbol are both valid spellings with different stress. Balompié is also valid, though less common.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Cirugía can refer to a surgical operation as well as the medical specialty.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Entero and íntegro fit complete with nothing missing; their other senses are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Bastante can be an adjective meaning enough, as well as an adverb. The enough sense fits here.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Uso, empleo and utilización fit application in the sense of putting something to use; not every sense of aplicación is interchangeable.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Período and periodo fit a span of time; temporada can also mean a season for an activity.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Alternativa can name an option; opción is also used for the act or ability of choosing.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Auxilio and asistencia fit help or aid; asistencia also means attendance in other contexts.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Juntar fits bringing things together; unir can also emphasize joining or attachment.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Forzar and obligar can both express making someone do something: obligar/forzar a alguien a hacer algo.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Parecer as a noun can mean an opinion, especially in a mi parecer. It is also a verb.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Gozar and disfrutar overlap for enjoyment; their complements may use de: gozar de algo, disfrutar de algo.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Similar, parecido and semejante express similarity. Usual constructions include similar a, parecido a and semejante a.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Pormenor is a detail, often in a fuller or more formal account.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Recolectar fits collecting; reunir fits gathering. Recoger also means picking up or retrieving something.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Subida and alza can name a rise in prices, like aumento and incremento.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Convidar can mean invite; its frequency and preferred uses vary by region.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Igual and igualmente can both mean in the same way. Igual has other adjectival and adverbial senses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Pelea and combate fit a fight; lucha also covers a sustained struggle.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Pieza can name a room in a dwelling; habitación and cuarto also fit that sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Vecindario can name a neighbourhood or its inhabitants; barrio names the district.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Hondo and profundo overlap for physical depth. Their figurative uses need their own context.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Incorporar fits bringing parts into a whole; integrar emphasizes making them part of that whole.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Reír and reírse both mean laugh. Reírse de can mean laugh at someone or something.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: The conventional Spanish file-menu label is Guardar como. This cue tests that label, not every possible use of save.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Permitir fits the permit sense; aprobar also means approving something or passing an exam.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Número fits number and dígito fits digit; cifra can have either sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Listado and lista both name a list; listado can also be a participle in other contexts.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Campo fits a field of activity; alcance fits scope or extent. Ámbito can express either in context.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Apropiado fits adequate in the sense of suitable or appropriate; enough in quantity would call for a different cue.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Norteamericano is also used for someone or something from the United States, although it can refer to North America more broadly. Estadounidense is geographically more precise.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Despacho can name an office room; oficina can also mean an administrative workplace.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Añadir, agregar and incluir fit adding something to a whole; incorporar and integrar emphasize making it part of that whole.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Perito is an expert, often in a technical or legal field. Experto is the broader term.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Niño fits boy when the young person is a child. Muchacho and chico can also refer to adolescents or young men.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Naturalmente and ciertamente fit naturally or certainly. Claro also means clearly in habla claro.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Breve fits short duration or a short text; corto also covers physical length.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Atención fits attention or care directed to someone or something; cuidado has other uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Septiembre and setiembre are both valid; regional preferences differ.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Representante fits someone acting for another person; agente has additional professional senses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Indumentaria fits clothing collectively; ropa is the ordinary general term.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Muro and pared overlap for a wall. Muro often suggests substantial construction but is not limited to outdoor walls.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Prevenir fits taking steps to prevent an event; impedir and evitar also fit stopping it from happening.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Fomentar and impulsar fit encouraging or advancing something; promover has other institutional uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Usual, común, normal and habitual overlap for customary rather than exceptional.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Cabello names hair on the human head; pelaje names an animal’s coat of fur. Both fit a sense explicitly shown here.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Expandir fits the expand sense; extender has additional senses and constructions.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Exactamente and precisamente overlap for precisely or exactly; precisely can also introduce an emphasis.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Exhibir, exponer and mostrar fit displaying artworks publicly; exponer also means explaining or exposing something.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Postura fits an attitude or stance; it can also describe bodily posture.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Video and vídeo are both correct; vídeo is usual in Spain and video in much of America.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Convertir fits changing something’s form or nature, commonly convertir algo en otra cosa.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Establecer and determinar fit setting or establishing something; fijar also means fastening it physically.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Además, también and asimismo can add information. They do not occupy every sentence position interchangeably.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Recientemente fits recently. Recién usually precedes a participle; in much of America it also accompanies finite verbs.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Millar is a group of a thousand; mil can also function as a numeral.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Dorso can refer to the back; espalda is the usual everyday term for a person’s back.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Discusión can mean a debate or discussion, not only an argument.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Lote can name a building plot; parcela and terreno also fit a tract of land.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Propulsar fits propelling something; impulsar also has figurative encouragement uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Conducta and comportamiento both describe behavior; their specialized uses depend on context.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Complicado can describe something composed of many pieces as well as something difficult to understand.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Ofrecimiento names an offer; oferta also has commercial senses such as a special offer.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Crimen fits crime; it often suggests a serious offense. Delito covers offenses more broadly.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Progreso and adelanto fit advance in the progress sense; adelanto can also mean an advance payment.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Rapidez fits ordinary speed. In physics and some fixed expressions, velocidad and rapidez have more specific uses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Conciencia and consciencia are both valid for awareness. Moral conscience is normally conciencia.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Actuación and interpretación overlap for an actor’s performance of a role. A whole show can instead be an espectáculo or función.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Desventaja and inconveniente fit disadvantage; objeción fits objection. In los pros y los contras, contra has a fixed noun use.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Rellenar can mean fill completely as well as refill or fill in a form.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Listo and preparado fit ready; dispuesto also expresses willingness.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Huir fits fleeing or escaping; escapar and escaparse both fit escape. Their uses are not identical in every sentence.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Aseo can mean a bathroom, particularly in Spain; baño also means a bath.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Remedio can mean a medicine or treatment; medicina also names the field of medicine.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Signo can mean a sign; letrero fits a written sign. Señal also includes a signal or indication.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Meter and insertar fit the insertion sense; introducir also means bringing something in or introducing it.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Arreglar and reparar fit the repair sense of componer, not its musical-composition sense.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Media and promedio overlap for an average, especially an arithmetic mean.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Arribo means arrival and can sound formal; llegada is the usual broad term.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Adinerado fits rich in money; sabroso fits tasty. These alternatives correspond to different senses of rico.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Tratar and discutir fit addressing or discussing a topic; discutir need not mean quarrelling.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Preservar fits keeping documents protected and in good condition.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Transmitir fits conveying a message; comunicar also has interpersonal and connecting senses.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Averiguar involves investigating to find something out and often emphasizes the result. Investigar and indagar emphasize the inquiry.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Usual, común, normal and habitual overlap for customary rather than exceptional.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Remedio can mean a medicine or treatment; medicamento specifically names a medicinal substance or preparation.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Valorar can mean evaluate or assess, as well as value or appreciate.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Comercio can name a shop; carpa is used for a tent in much of America. These fit different senses of tienda.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Encomendar fits entrusting a task; encargar also means ordering goods or commissioning work.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Entrar fits enter and depositar fits depositing money; ingresar also means joining an institution.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Presente as a noun fits the current time. Actualidad can also mean current affairs.

sections.title: Meaning and alternatives
sections.text: Legal can mean relating to law, as well as lawful. Jurídico usually selects the relating-to-law sense.
